Mixed-Design Multivariate ANOVA With All Four Test Statistics

Source: R/manova_split_plot.R
manova_split_plot.Rd

Computes the multivariate analysis of variance for a mixed-design (one between-subjects factor and one within-subjects factor), returning Wilks's \(\Lambda\), Pillai's trace, Hotelling-Lawley trace, and Roy's largest root, each with the associated F-approximation, degrees of freedom, and p-value. The three effects, between-subjects (A), within-subjects (B), and the interaction (\(A \times B\)), are tested separately, following the multivariate approach to the split-plot design of Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley (2027, Section 14.6). Wraps Anova and returns the result in the tidy DMAR style.

Usage

manova_split_plot(data, within, between, ss_type = 3L)

Arguments

data

A data.frame in wide format, one row per subject, with the within-subjects measurements in separate columns and the between-subjects factor as one additional column.

within

Character vector of column names holding the repeated measures values (one column per level of the within- subjects factor). Must be in the canonical level order.

between

Character name of the between-subjects factor column in data.

ss_type

The sum-of-squares type, passed through to Anova. Accepts the integers 1, 2, or 3 or the equivalent Roman-numeral strings "I", "II", or "III", and defaults to 3L (Type III). With one between-subjects factor the type matters only for the within-subjects main effect when the groups differ in size: Type III tests the unweighted grand means of the within-subjects contrasts and Type II the weighted grand means (see Details). The chosen type is recorded in the returned table (see Value). Type I (1 or "I") is not available for this mixed design, because Anova computes only Type II and Type III sums of squares for the multivariate repeated measures path; requesting it raises an error.

Value

A data.frame (class dmar_tbl) with rows for each of the three effects crossed with each of the four multivariate statistics, plus one trailing row recording the sum-of-squares type. Columns: effect, statistic_name, statistic_value, F_approx, df_1, df_2, p_value. The final row has effect == "sum_of_squares_type" and carries the chosen type (2 or 3) in its numeric statistic_value; its remaining numeric columns are NA, so the statistic_value column stays numeric. The table prints through the dmar_tbl display layer: whole numbers such as the degrees of freedom without a decimal part, the statistics to 3 decimal places, and p-values to 4 decimal places (one below 0.0001 prints as “< 0.0001”); the stored values keep full precision. tidy() gives one row per row of the table, its term joining effect and statistic_name and its estimate the statistic_value, so the final row is the term "sum_of_squares_type:NA" (its statistic_name is NA) with the type as its estimate; glance() gives one row, the number of rows (n_terms) with conf_level and B_used NA, since no interval or bootstrap is formed (see dmar_tidiers). as.data.frame() returns the table as a plain data.frame.

Details

The three tests. The multivariate approach replaces each subject's \(b\) repeated measures with transformed variables: their mean \(M\), and \(b - 1\) contrasts among them, the \(D\) variables. The between-subjects effect (A) is the one-way ANOVA of \(M\) across the \(a\) groups (Maxwell, Delaney, & Kelley, 2027, Equation 14.40), which is also the univariate approach's test of A. The interaction (\(A \times B\)) asks whether the groups differ in their means on the \(D\) variables, a one-way MANOVA of the \(D\) variables (their Equations 14.62 and 14.63). The within-subjects main effect (B) asks whether the grand means of the \(D\) variables are all zero, averaging over the groups (their Equation 14.54). Both within-subjects tests take as their error matrix the pooled within-group sums of squares and cross-products of the \(D\) variables, and no test depends on which \(b - 1\) contrasts are formed. A test of B within a single group is a simple effect (their Section 14.7.4), a different question from the main effect.

Weighted or unweighted grand means. When the groups differ in size, the grand mean of a \(D\) variable can be the unweighted average of its \(a\) group means or the average weighted by group size, which is its mean over all N subjects; the two agree when the groups are of equal size, and the choice affects only the test of B. Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley (2027, Section 14.6.9, p. 796, and Chapter 14, note 6, p. 854) generally prefer the unweighted means, which they note SAS and SPSS test by default, while allowing that the weighted means suit some studies. The sum-of-squares type selects between them. Type III (the default) tests the unweighted grand means: the between-subjects factor is coded with sum-to-zero contrasts, whatever options("contrasts") says, so that the intercept of the regression of each \(D\) variable on the groups is the unweighted mean of its group means, and the hypothesis matrix is \(a \tilde{n} \bar{D}_U \bar{D}_U^\top\), where \(\bar{D}_U\) holds the unweighted grand means and \(\tilde{n}\) is the harmonic mean of the group sizes (their notes 10 and 14). Type II tests the weighted grand means \(\bar{D}\), with the hypothesis matrix \(N \bar{D} \bar{D}^\top\) (their note 11). Under R's default treatment coding, the intercept would instead be the first group's means, and its Type III test the simple effect of B in the first group (their Equation 14.66). With one between-subjects factor, the two types give the same tests of A and of the interaction, and with equal group sizes the same test of B as well. Type I, the sequential decomposition, is not available here: Anova computes only Type II and Type III for the multivariate repeated measures path. The type in force is reported in the returned table so the analysis is self-documenting.

The four statistics. For an effect with \(H\) and \(E\) hypothesis- and error-cross-products matrices:

  • Wilks's \(\Lambda = \det(E) / \det(E + H)\)

  • Pillai's trace \(V = \mathrm{tr}(H (E + H)^{-1})\)

  • Hotelling-Lawley trace \(T_0^2 = \mathrm{tr}(H E^{-1})\)

  • Roy's largest root \(\theta = \lambda_1(H E^{-1})\)

When to use which. For many data sets the four statistics are likely to reach the same conclusion about statistical significance, but that agreement is not guaranteed, and without more information about the population than is usually available none of them can be said to be best. Wilks's \(\Lambda\) is historically the most widely used, and there is some evidence that Pillai's trace is the most robust of the four (Maxwell, Delaney, & Kelley, 2027, Section 14.6.11). Roy's largest root uses only the largest eigenvalue of \(H E^{-1}\), the largest ratio of hypothesis to error variation over linear combinations of the transformed variables. The four statistics give the same F whenever \(s = 1\), where \(s\) is the smaller of the number of transformed variables and the effect's degrees of freedom for each of them (Maxwell, Delaney, & Kelley, 2027, Section 14.6.11): always for A and B, and for the interaction when either factor has two levels.

Dependency. Requires the car package on CRAN.

References

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge. (See Chapter 14, Section 14.6, on the multivariate approach to split-plot designs, and Chapter 7, Sections 7.9 and 7.10, on weighted and unweighted marginal means.)

Rencher, A. C., & Christensen, W. F. (2012). Methods of multivariate analysis (3rd ed.). Wiley. doi:10.1002/9781118391686

Examples

# Two groups of ten measured at three times. Both groups start at the
# same place and rise over time, and group B rises twice as fast, so the
# data generating means differ in slope as well as in level.
set.seed(113)
n_per <- 10
d <- data.frame(
  subject = factor(1:(2 * n_per)),
  group   = factor(rep(c("A", "B"), each = n_per)),
  t1      = c(rnorm(n_per, 0,   1), rnorm(n_per, 0,   1)),
  t2      = c(rnorm(n_per, 0.4, 1), rnorm(n_per, 0.8, 1)),
  t3      = c(rnorm(n_per, 0.8, 1), rnorm(n_per, 1.6, 1))
)

# Rows are the between-subjects effect (labeled A), the within-subjects
# main effect (labeled B), and their interaction, each with all four
# multivariate criteria, followed by a row recording the sum-of-squares
# type. The multivariate tests make no sphericity assumption, which is
# what recommends them over the univariate repeated measures F and its
# epsilon corrections.
manova_split_plot(d, within = c("t1", "t2", "t3"), between = "group")
#>  effect              statistic_name   statistic_value F_approx df_1 df_2
#>  A                   Pillai           0.085           1.681    1    18  
#>  A                   Wilks            0.915           1.681    1    18  
#>  A                   Hotelling-Lawley 0.093           1.681    1    18  
#>  A                   Roy              0.093           1.681    1    18  
#>  B                   Pillai           0.552           10.469   2    17  
#>  B                   Wilks            0.448           10.469   2    17  
#>  B                   Hotelling-Lawley 1.232           10.469   2    17  
#>  B                   Roy              1.232           10.469   2    17  
#>  interaction         Pillai           0.082           0.761    2    17  
#>  interaction         Wilks            0.918           0.761    2    17  
#>  interaction         Hotelling-Lawley 0.090           0.761    2    17  
#>  interaction         Roy              0.090           0.761    2    17  
#>  sum_of_squares_type <NA>             3               <NA>     <NA> <NA>

# With six subjects left in group A, the types differ in the B rows
# alone: Type III (the default) averages the two groups' changes over
# time equally, and Type II weights each group by its size.
d_unequal <- d[-(1:4), ]
manova_split_plot(d_unequal, within = c("t1", "t2", "t3"),
                  between = "group")
